title: Flu activity rises across US as 6 states reach high levels, CDC data shows
text:
The agency estimates 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations and 2,100 flu deaths so far this season

Flu cases on the rise early as medication purchases surge

Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses rising flu activity across the U.S. and advances in fertility treatment after actress Hilary Swank reportedly announced her third pregnancy at 52.

Cases of the flu are already cropping up across the country in an early spike.

In its weekly influenza update, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has alerted that seasonal flu activity is "higher than typically observed at this time of year."

About 11% of specimens tested for flu at clinical labs were positive in the week ending Nov. 7, with that percentage rising. The CDC also reported more than 3% of doctors’ office visits were due to flu-like symptoms.

WANT TO DODGE THE FLU THIS YEAR? EAT THESE SECRET-WEAPON IMMUNITY-BOOSTING FOODS

New York, Massachusetts and Hawaii were in the CDC map’s moderate category for influenza-like illness in the week ending Nov. 7 (week 44).

The CDC’s Outpatient Respiratory Illness Activity Map uses reports from ILINet, the agency’s national network of outpatient health care providers, to show how often patients are visiting doctors for respiratory illness symptoms. (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)

California, Tennessee and Oregon were in the high category for influenza-like illness, along with South Carolina and Texas. Louisiana was the only state in the very high category, according to the CDC’s Week 44 map.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The CDC noted that an earlier increase in activity does not predict a higher seasonal peak or overall severity.

While it’s too early to know which flu viruses will be most dominant this season, in the week ending Nov. 7, the most frequently reported virus was influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, a descendant of the strain that caused the 2009 swine flu pandemic and has circulated seasonally since.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The CDC estimates that there have been 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations and 2,100 deaths tied to flu infections so far this season. Five flu-associated deaths among children have been reported to the agency.

Cases of influenza are already on the rise across the U.S. this November. (iStock)

In an October media briefing, Dr. Anna Durbin of Johns Hopkins University stated that the flu hospitalization rate in mid-October was the highest it’s been in 15 years.

"Because the flu season is starting a bit earlier, I think it's really important for everyone to get a flu vaccine as soon as possible," she advised.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Dr. Fred Lopez, an infectious diseases specialist at the LSU Health Sciences Center in New Orleans, told the Associated Press that flu season is "taking off in a direction that’s only likely to increase in the next month or two."

"If you haven’t been vaccinated, you should get vaccinated now," he added.

The CDC recommends an annual seasonal flu vaccination, available for people 6 months and older. (iStock)

The CDC recommends an annual flu vaccine for everyone 6 months and older. Prescription antiviral drugs can treat flu and should be started as early as possible, especially for people at higher risk of complications.

With Thanksgiving approaching, doctors expect flu and other respiratory viruses to spread as people travel and gather with friends and family.

Last winter, flu activity surged in late December. At the time, New York City health officials described the season as the city’s most intense in 20 years, according to the AP.

Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.
